name: Mala (Papua New Guinea)
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Loeweke, Eunice & May, Jean 1982. Three languages of the Kaukombaran family (grammar sketch ms, SIL, covers Pay=Mala [ped]); PDF not publicly retrievable.

new_statements.quote: In all four languages stress is contrastive and thus phonemic. Examples of contrastive stress are as follows: [...] Mala /'umia/ 'be quiet' /u'mia/ 'you will die' /'baba/ 'older brother' /ba'bam/ 'possum' [...] An interesting feature of stress has been noted in comparing two syllable words that are similar in all four languages. Maia tends to stress the first syllable, whereas Maiani, Miani and Mala stress the second syllable. [...] /'ulum/ 'dirty' (Maia) /u'lum/ 'dirty' (Maiani, Mala)
new_statements.citation: May, Jean & Eunice Loeweke. 1985. A recommended alphabet for Maiani, Miani, Mala and Maia - four languages of the Kaukambaran language family. In John M. Clifton (ed.), Five phonological studies (Workpapers in Papua New Guinea Languages 31), 1-25. Ukarumpa: Summer Institute of Linguistics. [Corroborated verbatim by May 1994, Mala (Pay, Alam) Organised Phonology Data, SIL ms., p. 3: 'Stress is contrastive and thus phonemic.']
new_statements.locator: Section 4 'Stress', pp. 11-12 (PDF pp. 11-12); orthography note sec. 5.3, pp. 13-14. OPD: 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)', p. 3.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in Mala is lexically contrastive (phonemic), demonstrated by segmentally identical pairs differing only in stress placement ('umia vs u'mia, 'baba vs ba'bam); as a tendency, disyllables cognate across the family carry second-syllable stress in Mala (as in Maiani and Miani), against initial stress in Maia. Stress is not marked in the practical orthography.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in either source.
new_statements.exceptions: The second-syllable placement is given only as a tendency for comparable two-syllable words; the minimal pairs themselves show initial-stressed disyllables exist ('baba, 'umia). Sec. 5.3: only 'a couple of words' are ambiguous in writing because stress is unwritten. No tone or vowel length reported (OPD suprasegmentals section mentions stress only).
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern isolated words/citation forms (minimal pairs include inflected verb forms, e.g. u'mia 'you will die'); no discussion of phrase-level prominence or of stress shifting under affixation.
new_statements.identity_note: Both primary sources treat Mala = Z'graggen's 'Pay' (OPD header: 'Mala (Pay, Alam) Language [PED]'; villages Busip, Tobenam, Dugumor, Aidebal, Malala, Moro), i.e. exactly Glottolog mala1494 / ISO ped. The 1985 paper covers four Kaukombaran languages jointly (Maiani tnh, Miani pla, Mala ped, Maia sks); the stress statement is made for all four with Mala-specific minimal pairs, and the second-syllable tendency is stated for Maiani, Miani and Mala as against Maia.

sources.note: p. 3 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)': 'Stress is contrastive and thus phonemic. Examples are as follows: 'umia 'be quiet' / u'mia 'you will die'; 'baba 'older brother' / ba'bam possum'. p. 3-4: /r/ is a flap between vowels in unstressed syllables; p. 4 'Conventions: Orthographic': 'Phonemic stress is not written.' No tone or length mentioned.

sources.citation: May, Jean & Eunice Loeweke. 1985 [written Feb. 1982]. A recommended alphabet for Maiani, Miani, Mala and Maia - four languages of the Kaukambaran language family. In John M. Clifton (ed.), Five phonological studies (Workpapers in Papua New Guinea Languages 31), 1-25. Ukarumpa: SIL. (SIL archive entry 23683; image-only scan, scanned at 300 dpi)
sources.note: Sec. 4 'Stress' (pp. 11-12): in all four languages stress is contrastive/phonemic; Mala pairs /'umia/ 'be quiet' vs /u'mia/ 'you will die', /'baba/ 'older brother' vs /ba'bam/ 'possum'; in comparable disyllables Maiani, Miani and Mala stress the second syllable whereas Maia stresses the first. Sec. 5/5.3 (pp. 13-14): stress not written in the orthography; only 'a couple of words' are ambiguous because of stress. Sec. 2.4.2: r is a flap between vowels in unstressed syllables.

sources.note: Pay (= Mala) at sec. 2.22.21.11; Kaukombaran typological notes are segmental only. General methodological remark: 'The marking of stress has been omitted, since the stress patterning has not been well established yet.' No Mala-specific stress statement.
